name: Chinpill

lead: The chinpill is a community framework holding that how far the chin projects, and how tall it is, strongly shapes how attractive a face looks in profile. Followers use it to judge their own profiles and decide whether a chin change is worth pursuing.
Posts cite orthognathic profiles, SNA/SNB angles and reference lines such as the E-line. Clinically, chin position is a recognised part of facial balance, and genioplasty exists to alter it.

paras: Practitioners compare side-profile photos against reference lines, discuss rules of thumb such as the chin reaching past the nose, and weigh options: implants, sliding genioplasty, fillers, or broader jaw surgery.

Genioplasty commonly causes swelling and bruising and can cause temporary lip numbness; less often infection, implant displacement or nerve injury. Fillers are usually temporary. Forum threads also frame the topic in harsh terms.

angle.text: Followers use the chinpill to judge whether the chin is balanced with the nose and lips in profile. If it is not, genioplasty or fillers are the usual routes discussed to change projection.

lead: The chinpill is a looksmaxxing framework, also written chin pill and sometimes called the tall chinpill, which holds that chin projection and chin height are central to a face looking attractive, especially from the side.[1][2] Members use it to assess their own profile and to decide whether chin-focused changes would improve it. It belongs to the family of "pills" in community vocabulary, in which a single feature is treated as a major driver of appearance.

Threads on looksmax.org describe the ideal as a straight, orthognathic profile and cite cephalometric angles such as SNA and SNB, which describe the front-back position of the upper and lower jaws.[1][3] One thread argues that a strong ramus and chin can carry a face from any angle.[4]

Medically, chin position is addressed by genioplasty (also called mentoplasty), which can add or reduce projection and height using implants, a sliding bone cut or fillers.[5] Where the whole lower jaw sits behind the upper jaw, orthognathic surgery can reposition it, and genioplasty is one of its component procedures.[6]

paras: Proponents argue the chin is a decisive profile feature that is hard to alter without surgery, and that even small deviations from an ideal change perceived attractiveness.[1] A common rule of thumb in replies is that a chin which does not project past the nose counts as recessed.[1] One thread presents side-profile photographs aligned to the E-line, a reference line used in orthodontics and facial planning.[1][3]

A related thread, the "ramus and chin pill", claims a long ramus together with chin projection can compensate for a weaker maxilla.[4] A third thread promotes the "tall chinpill", pointing to chin height rather than projection alone.[2][7] Posts in these threads often combine chin discussion with talk of jaw-muscle training, hormones and jaw surgery.[4]

The chin is the forward-projecting part of the lower jaw (mandible) below the lower lip. Humans are the only primates with a chin, and researchers have proposed several explanations for why it evolved, none of them settled.[8] Asymmetric growth of the bony prominence at the chin can produce facial asymmetry, and a cleft chin is an inherited variant.[8]

Orthodontists and surgeons measure profile using lateral skull radiographs. The cephalostat, a device that standardises such images, was introduced by Holly Broadbent Sr. in 1931.[3] In Steiner analysis, SNA describes the front-back position of the upper jaw (average about 82 degrees) and SNB that of the lower jaw (average about 80 degrees); ANB, their difference, averages about 2 degrees and is used to classify jaw relationships.[3] The Ricketts E-line runs from the tip of the nose to the soft-tissue chin and is used as an aesthetic reference for lip position.[3] Posts in the community cite these terms, with slightly different ranges from the textbook averages.[1][3]

Genioplasty reshapes the chin. Options include implants of silicone, polyethylene or ePTFE placed through an incision under the chin or inside the lip; a sliding osteotomy in which a horseshoe-shaped piece of jawbone is moved forward or back and fixed with titanium plates; and reduction techniques that shorten or narrow the chin.[5] It is often performed together with rhinoplasty.[5]

Orthognathic surgery corrects jaw positions for bite, airway and appearance reasons, using procedures such as sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw and Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw, with genioplasty as a companion procedure.[6] Hyaluronic acid and similar fillers are used as a non-surgical, temporary way to add projection; this wiki's article on fillers covers them separately.

Reported effects of genioplasty include swelling, bruising and temporary lip numbness, with less common infection, bone changes, implant displacement or nerve injury; surgeon experience is described as reducing risk.[5] Orthognathic surgery carries reported infection rates of up to about 7 percent, along with bleeding and numbness that is usually temporary and rarely permanent; healing takes weeks to months.[6]

The chinpill thread titles use the same style as other community "pill" posts: short, emphatic and often illustrated with side-profile photographs.[1][2][7] Replies tend to add comparisons to other features such as the maxilla and ramus, and links to threads on jaw surgery.[4] Some posts describe the ideal profile as "straight" and rank other profile types below it.[1]

No studies found on the chinpill as a framework. Surgical and orthodontic literature on genioplasty, profile analysis and jaw surgery exists separately and is summarised in the reference works cited above.[5][6][3]

lore.intro: The theory circulates on looksmax.org in several threads about profile, ramus and chin height.[1][4][2]

claims.claim: A strong ramus and chin can save a face with a weak maxilla
A chin that does not project past the nose is recessed
Chin height (the "tall chinpill") is the key profile feature
The chin cannot be changed without surgery
Jaw training and hormones can build a strong ramus and chin

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes one of the first jaw-surgery cases later grouped under orthognathic surgery.[6]
Holly Broadbent Sr. introduces the cephalostat, standardising skull radiographs for profile measurement.[3]
A report on combined nose and chin surgery is published, cited in genioplasty references.[5]
looksmax.org threads on chin projection, ramus and tall chin height circulate.[1][4][2]
